Low window resolutions

Settings, VIDEO tab (desktop): window resolution now starts at 640x360, then 854x480, 960x540, 1024x576, 1280x720 and up to 5K. The cfg stores res_px=WxH; old res=<index> files are migrated to the same size. Picking a resolution clears the remembered window size so the choice always applies. On web and mobile the window follows the page, so use Render scale (down to 25%) instead.

Desktop, software rendering, perf tour (Kaito vs Shion): 1280x720 31.5 ms, 854x480 15.1 ms, 640x360 10.5 ms per frame. Web render scale 50% / 35% / 25%: 21.5 / 22.0 / 23.4 fps (CPU bound below 50%).

Web: stage thumbnails (1.4 MB, used only as the epilogue backdrop placeholder) are fetched on demand from assets/stages/thumbs/ instead of embedded: wasm 21.14 -> 19.77 MB, gzip 11.64 -> 10.26 MB (-11.8%).

Sprite Container (LZ4)

Every pixel block the engine stores for later use is LZ4-compressed, with one rule for both fighter kinds. Decoders are pure Rust (lz4_flex, safe mode, builds for wasm32), the format is lossless, and PNG stays the authoring format.

Formats

MagicHoldsWritten byRead by
UML1one sprite: indexed (8-bit + palette) or RGBAume-tools pack-sprites (web fighter packs)ume_formats::lz4_sprite, ume_native sprite loader
UMSFa whole .sff: palettes, sprite table, one UML1 block per distinct pixel bufferume-tools cook-sffume_formats::sff::decode_sff and decode_sff_only

Readers recognise the magic, so a PNG, a classic .sff and a cooked file are interchangeable under the same name. A cooked file can replace the original .sff in a character folder or zip.

UML1 layout (little endian)

"UML1"  kind u8 (0 RGBA, 1 indexed)  colors u16  width u16  height u16
crop x u16  crop y u16  crop w u16  crop h u16
palette: colors * 4 bytes (RGBA), indexed only
LZ4 block of the cropped pixels (absent when the crop is empty)

The crop removes only the border that is exactly zero (index 0, or RGBA 0,0,0,0), so decoding restores every byte. Colour hidden under zero alpha elsewhere is kept.

UMSF layout

"UMSF"  version u8 (1)  sff version u8  2 bytes zero
unique palettes   u32 count, each u32 length + bytes
palette table     u32 count, each group i32, index i32, palette ref u32
blocks            u32 count, each u32 length + UML1 bytes (no palette)
sprites           u32 count, each group, index, axis x, axis y i32; width, height u32;
                  palette_index i32; palette ref u32; block ref u32 (u32::MAX = none)

Sprites that shared one pixel buffer in the decoded .sff (links) share one block, and decode back to one shared Arc, so memory behaviour is unchanged. Blocks decode in parallel through ume_formats::par::map (single thread on wasm32). decode_sff_only skips blocks of sprites that are not wanted.

Limits

A sprite is at most 8192 px per side and 16 Mpx, and a UMSF file may declare at most 512 Mpx of wanted sprites. Counts and lengths are checked against the file size; truncated or corrupt files return an error and never panic.

Commands

cargo run --release -p ume-devtools --bin ume-tools -- cook-sff in.sff out.sff
cargo run --release -p ume-devtools --bin ume-tools -- pack-sprites web/dist

cook-sff decodes the original, cooks it, decodes the result and fails unless every palette and every sprite (pixels, axes, palette, links) is identical.

Measurements

62 real M.U.G.E.N. characters from mugen-assets (54,382 sprites), one thread, per-sprite blocks: LZ4 decodes at about 1.5 GB/s of indexed pixels, 28 µs per sprite against 61 µs for the original RLE8/LZ5 decode. Totals, original .sff against UMSF: 853.6 MB against 624.1 MB, decode 2.30 s against 1.42 s with the default worker count. The comparison with zstd, PNG8, QOI and deflate is in ADR 0009.

Web Match Smoke

node scripts/web-match-smoke.js web/dist plays complete matches in headless Chromium (CI job web-qa, after the web build) and fails when a match freezes.

Each scenario opens a deep link with ?e2e=1, which publishes window.__ume_state every frame (screen, clock.tick, round, wins, fighters). Settings are injected through localStorage (30 s rounds, 1.15x speed, muted).

ScenarioWhat it covers
cpu-bot-best-of-3A scripted player closes in and mashes attacks against the CPU for at least two rounds
watch-cpu-vs-cpuNo input: the match must still run to the results screen

A scenario fails on any of:

  • page error, Rust panic, RuntimeError or an unexpected console.error;
  • the simulation tick not advancing for MATCH_SMOKE_STALL_MS (default 20000 ms) outside pause and match end;
  • no animation frame, or an unresponsive main thread, for the same period;
  • the rendered image never changing during the fight;
  • the results screen not being reached within MATCH_SMOKE_LIMIT_MS (default 360000 ms), or not being leavable with Enter.

MATCH_SMOKE_SCENARIOS=<name,...> runs a subset, MATCH_SMOKE_SHARD=<i>/<n> runs every n-th scenario starting at i (CI splits the match smoke across parallel jobs this way; an empty selection fails) and WEB_SMOKE_SHOTS=<dir> stores screenshots (uploaded by CI on failure).

Web QA pipeline

Every pull request plays the real wasm build in headless Chromium, in parallel shards, and fails on any WebAssembly error. A failure leaves screenshots and logs as CI artifacts.

What runs

scripts/web-qa.json lists the scenarios; scripts/web-qa.js runs one shard of them. CI job web-qa (matrix of 8 parts, fail-fast: false, --jobs 2). Scenarios are spread over the parts by the durations in scripts/web-qa-weights.json (60 s when a scenario is not listed), so a new scenario needs no CI edit. --shard <name> still selects one group of the table below:

ShardScenarios
uititle to fight flow, Arcade click, story intro, epilogue
mobiletouch menu, touch controls in a fight, in-engine smoke on a Pixel 7 viewport
enginein-engine smoke (?smoke=1): boot, menus, select, training, 5v5, story; plus the guard self-test
loadingM.U.G.E.N import (kfm), native fighters with awakenings, power arena, audio unlock, fatal-trap screen (unreachable)
match-1, match-2full matches in two halves (Web match smoke)

The guard

Every scenario runs with scripts/web-guard.js preloaded. It watches every page and fails the run, even when the script itself forgot to, on:

  • panicked, PanicHookInfo, unreachable executed or renderbufferStorageMultisample in the console;
  • gpu error: (the wgpu error handler in ume-shell);
  • an uncaught pageerror or a Chromium crash.

On the first problems it saves problem-N.png immediately, and a final-N.png before the browser closes. It also writes console.log (every console line with the time and page) and network.log (failed requests and HTTP 400+). fatal-trap sets expectFatal because it throws a trap on purpose, so there the guard only records.

Artifacts

Each shard uploads web-qa-<shard> (always, kept 7 days): summary.md, summary.json and one folder per scenario with output.log, console.log, network.log, guard.json, shots/ and the .png files. The summary is also written to the job summary page with the failing problems and the last output lines.

Run it locally

./scripts/build-web.sh
npm install --no-save playwright@1.56.1 && npx playwright install chromium
node scripts/web-qa.js --dist web/dist --out web-qa-report --shard ui
node scripts/web-qa.js --only fatal-trap,engine-smoke --jobs 2

Software GL is slow: keep --jobs at 1 or 2 locally. For a one-off page add ?debug=1 and read the console.

Adding a scenario

  1. Write scripts/web-<name>-smoke.js that takes the dist folder as its first argument and exits non-zero on failure.
  2. Add it to scripts/web-qa.json with a shard, or list it under excluded with the reason (network, manual tool).

scripts/web-qa.test.mjs fails when a web-*-smoke.js is neither covered nor excluded, or when the part matrix in ci.yml does not cover every scenario exactly once.

Visual tour

node scripts/web-tour.js web/dist <out> walks title, menu, every utility screen, select, stages, VS, fight and pause with real keys and saves a numbered screenshot per step (TOUR_MOBILE=1 uses a phone in landscape, TOUR_LANG=pt-BR sets the browser locale). It fails on panics, navigation or browser errors, or a fight that never starts; the screenshots are for review and PR evidence.

Media capture

Screenshots and GIFs for the README come from the real web build running in headless Chromium, so what the docs show is what the game renders.

Steps

  1. rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown and cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli --locked --version <Cargo.lock version>.
  2. ./scripts/build-web.sh writes web/dist.
  3. node scripts/web-smoke.js web/dist must pass before any capture.
  4. CAPTURE_OUT=<dir> node scripts/web-capture.js <plan.json> plays a key plan and saves the results.

Plan file

{
  "video": "fight.webm",
  "steps": [
    { "key": "Enter", "wait": 900, "shot": "menu" },
    { "key": "ArrowDown" },
    { "hold": "ArrowRight", "ms": 600 },
    { "wait": 3000, "shot": "fight" }
  ]
}
  • key taps a key for hold frames (default 2) and waits wait ms (default 900).
  • hold with ms keeps a key down for that long.
  • shot saves <shot>.png after the step; video records the whole session as WebM.

Convert a WebM to a small GIF with ffmpeg -i fight.webm -vf "fps=20,scale=480:-1:flags=lanczos,split[a][b];[a]palettegen=max_colors=128[p];[b][p]paletteuse=dither=bayer:bayer_scale=3" fight.gif.

Automated Pipeline: record-gameplay.js & Skill

For automated recording of gameplay, milestone screenshots (1280x720) and Bayer-dithered GIFs in headless Linux environments:

node scripts/record-gameplay.js --out docs/evidence/<topic> --gif gameplay.gif --duration 6

See the complete guide in .agents/skills/ume-media-capture/SKILL.md.

Stress tests and resilience

What is covered

AreaTestCommand
Format parsers (SFF, AIR, INI/DEF/CNS/CMD, SND, ACT, PCX, PNG, zip, stage)Deterministic mutation fuzzer seeded from the bundled kfm zip. Fails on any panic or any input slower than 1.5 s.UME_FUZZ_ITERS=4000 cargo test -p ume-formats --release --test it fuzz::
Spawner spam (Explod, Projectile, Helper every tick)Tick cost stays boundedcargo test -p ume-engine --release --test it stress:: -- --nocapture
Hot pathsBuilt-in bench for SFF decode, AIR parse, CNS compile, char load, match tick with 2, 6 and 10 fighterscargo run -p ume-engine --release --example hotpath_bench
Rollback under latencycrates/netplay/tests/rollback.rs (in-memory sockets)cargo test -p ume-netplay

Findings and fixes

  • A corrupt SFF header could claim a 65535x65535 sprite: 3 to 48 s and gigabytes of RAM per file. Sprites and PNGs above 16M pixels (MAX_SPRITE_PIXELS) are now treated as empty.
  • Explods and projectiles had no cap. With Helpers spawning every tick, 240 ticks took 72 s and the cost grew quadratically (projectile pairs). Both are now capped at 256; extra spawns are dropped, as in MUGEN. 2000 ticks with 61 fighters now take 1.2 s (about 0.6 ms per tick).

Hot path numbers (kfm720, release, cloud CI-class CPU)

PathTime
SFF decode1.1 ms
AIR parse1.0 ms
CNS parse and compile3.2 ms
Char load without images7.6 to 10 ms
Match tick, 2 fighters5 us
Match tick, 6 fighters15 us
Match tick, 10 fighters39 us

The simulation is far below the 16.6 ms frame budget, so loading and rendering are the places to optimize, not the tick.

Comparison and ideas not done yet

  • GGRS provides SyncTestSession (resimulate every frame and compare checksums) and desync detection; bevy_ggrs documents a desync debugging workflow. Running a sync test in CI over a scripted fight would catch non-determinism early.
  • Ikemen GO added rollback netcode through GGPO-style save/load of full game state; the cost driver there is state size, so keeping fighters free of large per-tick allocations (already tested in tick_alloc) matters.
  • Not covered yet: packet loss and jitter in the netplay harness (only latency), GPU device-lost recovery, low-memory behavior, a CNS/expression fuzzer in the engine crate, and a roster stress that loads many different characters.

Native animation coverage

This delivery completes dedicated pose art for the native roster: every animation frame the engine can name resolves to its own PNG file. The shared numbered canvases (09_hit1, 13_fall2, ...) keep serving their legacy aliases, and purely procedural effect frames (boltHit, beams) stay engine-rendered by design; both are approved resolutions, not gaps.

Included in this wave

  • Dedicated portrait.png images for all sixteen native fighters remain in place for roster tiles and HUD portraits.
  • Every string pose referenced by an animation now has a dedicated PNG in assets/chars/sprites/<id>/, including the guard, crouch, jump, flip, turn, land, win, intro, taunt, df* defeat set, and the previously idle-reusing low-hit poses. Inline pose objects have their inline_<hash> frame rendered once.
  • Dedicated PNGs must be generated in arcade pixel art via generate_image using a validated canonical anchor of the fighter (the deprecated vector-rig generate_missing_sprites tool has been removed). Write 400×400 RGBA frames with axis (200, 392) and refHeight 320 metadata, matching the existing convention.
  • Verification: cargo run --release -p ume-engine --example native_sprite_audit -- <out.json> --require-complete must pass for every fighter, and cargo run --release -p ume-devtools --bin ume-tools -- audit-sprites --out <report.json> must stay clean on geometry and alpha edges. cargo run --release -p ume-devtools --bin ume-tools -- audit-moves is the static roster audit (inputs, cancels, throws, hit boxes).

sprite-gen QA loop

The sprite-gen skill remains the tool of record for art quality QA on the native loops, with no image-generation credentials required:

  • ume-tools motion-descriptor --character assets/chars/<id>.json --sprites assets/chars/sprites/<id> --animation walk --out walk.json
  • sprite-gen inspect-motion --source walk.json --out walk-report.json measures anchors, duplicate frames, bbox drift and edge contact; foot contact needs explicit --contacts and --foot-box inputs.
  • ume-tools preview-motion and ume-tools preview-scene render review GIFs and MP4s with the sprite-gen stages. See Sprite Atlas Import for the component-row import path when AI-generated art is wanted.

Known limits

Inventory and audit reports do not prove that the animations play naturally in a match: state triggers, transition smoothness and hitbox fit must still be validated in Training. Recolors apply at load time through the palette system, so visual spot checks should cover every palette of a fighter, not just the first one.

M.U.G.E.N character code study

Read-only study of public M.U.G.E.N packages: Goku GT (Fighter Factory pack from the project folder) and four Mortal Kombat Project 4.9.3 fighters (Scorpion UMK3, Sub-Zero UMK3, Liu Kang, Shao Kahn) fetched from archive.org. Only text files (.def, .cmd, .cns, .st) were extracted and read; nothing was executed and no art, audio or code was copied into the repository.

Package shapes

PackageCode sizeStatedefsLayout
Goku GT~31k lines~175cmd + cns + Especiales, Supers, SS1..SS4 (one file per form), IA for Statedef -2/-3
Scorpion UMK323.6k2211.cmd, 1.cns, Basic_Moves.st, Sp.st, Combos.st, finishers
Sub-Zero UMK328.4k324same plus 2.st, 3.st (alternate moves), Stage_Finishers.st
Liu Kang19.4k161Special_Punches.st for the kick/punch specials
Shao Kahn27.0k262Bmoves.st, Sp.st, helpers (100 Helper controllers)

Patterns

  1. Short motion commands. MK characters use 2 to 3 step inputs (B,B,a, D,F,x, F,F,b) instead of quarter circles, with time windows around 10 ticks. UMF accepts the same notation in moves[].input.
  2. Fast, long moves = helpers. Scorpion's spear is a Helper (state 1010) spawned on animelem = 4, with DestroySelf at time = 150, and the owner waits in state 1000 until p2stateno is the pull state (1020/1021), then switches to 1001 to pull. In UMF this is a projectile plus a throw follow-up.
  3. Teleports. Scorpion's 1100 (behind) and 1200 (forward) are plain PosSet/PosAdd states; UMF has teleport frame or abilities.teleport.
  4. Specials per button. One motion, a different button picks the variant (Liu Kang F,F plus x, a, b or y: fireball, flying kick, bicycle kick, etc.). UMF equivalent: one move per button plus EX versions.
  5. Heavy explod use. 440 to 530 Explod controllers per character for sparks, ice, fire and blood; UMF handles these through spark, hitAnim and fx.
  6. Combos stored in states. Combos.st holds scripted chains. UMF models this with cancels routes.
  7. AI as input scripts. 100+ commands named AI001.. (long button sequences) drive the computer opponent. UMF uses the built-in AI instead of per-character command scripts.
  8. Finishers (fatality, brutality, pit) are separate states keyed off round end; not migrated.

Fast versus strong in these kits

  • Fast: Sub-Zero slide (B,F,a kick) and rolls (F,F,F, B,B,B), Scorpion teleports and spear; low damage per hit, cancels into specials.
  • Strong: Shao Kahn hammer and crab specials (F,F,b, D,F,b), armor through long recovery, command attacks (B,F,y run punch).

These map to the lunge, falcondive, shoulder and meteordrop moves added to the native roster, see Fighter study.

Census: how much of a package is repetition

ume-tools mugen-census <zip-or-dir>... (crates/devtools/src/mugen_census.rs) reads only the text files of a package (.cns, .st, .cmd, .air) and counts states, controllers, commands and animation actions. Three packages measured, nothing extracted or copied:

PackageCode filesCode linesStatedefsCommon states redeclaredControllersCommandsAI commandsAIR actions
Goku GT (DBFZ style)1135092329563114782529
Goku UI (DBFZ style)727742258682241782294
Kung Fu Man (bundled)61064611810711740234
ControllerUsesShareUMF equivalent
changestate99716%generated from cancels, when and move kind
playsnd81313%voice and per-level hit sounds
explod5529%fx, spark, hitAnim
velset3526%vel on frames
helper3115%projectile, throw, abilities
hitdef2724%hits[]
changeanim2494%anim per move
destroyself2244%projectile removeTime

What the numbers say:

  1. A fighter is 10k to 35k lines of code, and the eight controllers above are 61% of all controller blocks. Every one of them is something UMF generates from a field instead of a hand-written state.
  2. Common states are copied and edited by hand. Each package redeclares 10 to 68 of the engine's common states (stand, walk, jump, guard, get-hit) to tweak them. UMF fighters never touch them: the differences are fields in stats and anims.
  3. Variants are full copies. EX and form versions of a move are whole new statedefs. In UMF a variant is one entry with "use": "<move>" and the fields that change.
  4. Nothing is shared between packages. Two Goku packages by the same author family share no file. UMF has extends and kits, so a new fighter can inherit a whole fighter or a move pack and stay in sync with it.

The same measurement on the native roster (21 fighters, 652 moves): 355 moves have a body identical to a move of another fighter, and 1136 of 1535 animations equal the most common version of that animation. That duplication is what extends, use and kits remove, see Reuse. The example fighter docs/examples/umf/mika.json is 671 bytes and plays with 40+ moves.

Limits

UMF cannot yet express scripted finishers, stage interactions (pit) or AI command scripts. Life conditions are now available through requires (see UMF character).

Dissection of four M.U.G.E.N fighters

Read-only study of four public packs, taken apart file by file with tools/mugen2umf: Aizen TYBW (Fighter Factory Ultimate, SFF v2), Gogeta SSJ4 (Pocket_Danyell and Sarevok), Goku SSJ GT (Yamcha Z) and Goku SSJ4 (_Vision). The packs are third-party files: nothing from them is committed, only what we learned. Companion studies: M.U.G.E.N code study and Fighter study.

Take-aways: Clsn2 outnumbers Clsn1 about 5 to 1 everywhere, because the body is split into 4 to 6 small boxes per frame (head, torso, arms, legs) and the attack is one to three boxes. This is the same rule as the native hit box audit.

File layout

FileRoleSeen in
.def[Info] name and author, [Files] list, pal1..pal12, pal.defaultsall
.cmd[Remap], [Defaults] (command.time, command.buffer.time), [Command] list, [Statedef -1] input to state routingall
.cns[Data], [Size], [Velocity], [Movement] constants then statesall
st1..st3 extra state filesIA.cns (-2/-3 AI), Especials.cns, Supers.cns, -final, -story-introsAizen, Goku SSJ4

.airActions: frames group,image,x,y,ticks[,flip,trans], Clsn1 (attack) Clsn2 (hurt), Clsn2Default, Loopstartall
.sff / .sndSprites and sound banks, referenced by group,image and group,indexall

Constants worth copying

  • Walk 2.3 to 2.4 forward, run 4.6, jump -8.1 to -10.1, yaccel .43 to .44, airjuggle 15, ground width 15 (10 for the thin Aizen), height 60, attack.dist 160. The native roster already uses the same scale.
  • fall.defence_up 50, liedown.time 60, sparkno -1 when the pack draws its own sparks.
  • Aizen sets airjump.num = 6 and a walk of 7: a fast "floaty" movement type, built from constants only.

Command layer

  • Quarter circles ~D, DF, F, a, half circles ~B, DB, D, DF, F, a, charge ~60$D,U,a and ~60$B,F,a (Goku SSJ), double taps FF, BB, ~D,U for super jump, 3-button combos a+b.
  • Button routing: /$B,x, /$D,y style commands hold a direction while pressing, giving command normals.
  • Buffers: command.time = 10 and buffer.time 1 in most packs, 15 to 30 for the packs that favour easy inputs.
  • Specials keyed off one motion, one button each: Aizen D,DF,F with a, b or c is Silent Slash, Dark Waves or Kurohitsugi. UMF does the same with one move per button.
  • Gogeta and Goku SSJ4 keep ai..ai13 commands (button strings) that only set an AI flag in -2; the engine has its own AI, so they are not migrated.
  • Cancels are written as extra triggers on the target move: trigger2 = numhelper(700) > 0 (Aizen cancels into specials while his clone lives), movehit and movecontact (165 uses in Aizen, 22 in Gogeta, 14 in Goku SSJ4). UMF names the same idea cancels and rekka.

Normal attack numbers

Standing light (200), standing heavy (210), crouching light (400), crouching heavy (410), jumping light (600), jumping heavy (610). Values are damage of the hit, pausetime of attacker and defender, ground.hittime, juggle points and poweradd:

StateGogetaGoku SSJGoku SSJ4Aizen
200 stand light20, pause 4,5, hit 11, juggle 4, power 2223, pause 7,8, hit 11, juggle 1, power 2023, pause 5,8, hit 7, juggle 1, power 2020, pause 9,9, hit 15, juggle 2, power 40
210 stand heavy55, pause 4,5, hit 1155, pause 11,11, hit 15, juggle 4, power 6063, pause 12,12, hit 15, juggle 5, power 6530, pause 9,9, hit 15

Rules the packs follow: light normals pause 4 to 8 ticks and give 15 to 25 power, heavy normals pause 11 to 12 and give 55 to 70, ground hittime 11 to 15, crouching lows use guardflag = L and ground.type = Low, jump normals use HA, and the heavy crouch is the sweep (Trip plus fall = 1, Goku SSJ).

Sound and sprite organisation

  • Sprites: group 0 idle, 20 walk, 40 jump, 100 and 105 turn and crouch start, 200 to 240 stand attacks, 400 crouch, 600 jump, 5000 to 5120 get-hit, 9000 portrait, 9000,1 small portrait. Specials use free groups from 1000 up. Goku SSJ4 keeps 121 groups for 198 images, Gogeta has 523 images in 109 groups (63 linked, sharing pixels).
  • Sounds: group 0 attack whooshes and voices, 5 hits, 6 guard, 11 KO, 20 and above for specials. Aizen has 104 sounds in group 0 alone.
  • Palettes: pal1..pal12 in the .def; Goku SSJ4 ships 5 .act, Gogeta 5, Aizen embeds its palettes in the SFF v2.
  • Timing: a normal is 8 to 17 ticks in total (Goku SSJ4 stand light 4 + 11 + 2, Aizen 2 + 2 + 4 + 4, Gogeta stand heavy 2 + 4 + 2); the hit frame is the middle one.

What the dissection changed in UME

  1. Native fighters must read like these packs: chain normals, rekka follow ups, command normals, air versions, one projectile per button, teleport, counter and a form.
  2. Hit and hurt boxes follow the limb: 3 hurt boxes minimum, attack boxes only where the frame has pixels (see the native hit box audit).
  3. Frame data targets the table above: light 4 to 8 tick pause, heavy 11 to 12, ground hit time 11 to 15.
  4. The Captain Marlow rebuild (see Characters) is the first fighter made with this method, see Remaking a M.U.G.E.N fighter as UMF.

No art, sprite or code from these games is used.

Patterns turned into engine features

  1. Dash attacks and armored charges (lunge, shoulder) as command normals that still cancel into specials.
  2. Air dives with angled velocity and ground bounce (falcondive, meteordrop).
  3. Specials that cancel into other specials through explicit cancels routes.
  4. Invulnerable anti-airs (invuln) and one-hit armor on slow, heavy moves.
  5. Fast fighters trade damage for mobility (low hitstun normals, superSpeed, teleport); strong fighters gain armor, wallBounce and heavy level hits.

Applied to the native roster

GroupFightersNew moves
FastJin, Akio, Lian, Suzume, Kaname, Haruki, Kaito, Voltalunge (F+y, dash strike, 115 % of the heavy punch, cancels into specials) and falcondive (air F+b, angled dive)
StrongBruno, Garan, Daichi, Valdricshoulder (F+y, one-hit armor, wall bounce, 120 % damage) and meteordrop (air F+b, ground bounce, 130 % damage)

Only data and moves changed: no sprite, pose or stage was touched; every move reuses an existing animation.

How these fighters are made from scratch

  1. Design the kit: normals (light, medium, heavy, crouching, air), 3-4 specials, 1-2 supers, throw, dash.
  2. Art: pixel art in Aseprite or GraphicsGale with one shared palette (index 0 transparent), 3D prerender with an orthographic camera, or emulator rips. Crop tight and set the axis on the feet.
  3. Package: Fighter Factory loads PCX/PNG into an SFF; a .air file sets frames and Clsn boxes; .cmd holds inputs; .cns holds states.
  4. Frame data: light normals startup 3-5 ticks, heavies 8-14; hitstop 9-13 ticks.
  5. Balance and test: training mode with hitboxes, combo routes, AI.

See .agents/skills/mugen-character-creator and .agents/skills/mugen-to-ume-migrator.

  • SRK wiki, Dustloop, StrategyWiki KOF XIII, MKKomplete, Fighters Generation, MUGEN Guild.

Fighting game research: opportunities

English · Português (BR)

🇧🇷 Pesquisa de recursos públicos de outros jogos de luta e lista priorizada de melhorias. Nada aqui está implementado ainda.

This page compares publicly known features of modern 2D and 2.5D fighters with the current state of Ultimate MUGEN and ranks concrete opportunities. It is a planning document: no feature listed here is implemented yet. Only publicly documented features are cited, and no third-party assets are copied.

Effort scale: S under 2 days, M about 1 week, L 2 to 4 weeks, XL over a month.

Suggested sequence

  1. Training toolkit (1, 2, 13), because every other feature is easier to verify with it.
  2. Netcode UI and online screen (4, 3), then replays (9).
  3. Tutorial and trials (5, 6), then accessibility and modern controls (8, 7).
  4. Select and results polish (11, 12), then modes (14, 15).
  5. Ranked service and spectator (10, 16) once lobbies are stable.
  6. Screenpack rendering (21) as a separate track.

Notes and caveats

  • Ikemen GO is credited as inspiration only, like in the Home page.
  • Feature lists reflect public information about each game as of the research date and may change with patches. Treat them as reference points, not requirements.
  • Input history and frame data tools (2) must read the match state only; they must not change the simulation, to keep rollback determinism.
  • Anything that adds fields to Match should also be included in ume_netplay::checksum.

Story mode research notes

What was found (fan wikis and reviews, not an official guide) and how it maps to the engine.

  • Final Fight (arcade, 1989). Six rounds plus two bonus rounds, a boss at the end of each round: Damnd (Slums), Sodom (Subway/Park), Edi. E (West Side; one source lists Andore and Edi. E together), Rolento (Industrial Area), Abigail (Bay Area) and Belger (Uptown). Thugs come in waves, weapons and food are picked up along the way.
  • Capcom Arcade Stadium. Rewind, save states, slow-down/turbo and adjustable difficulty; credits are effectively unlimited.
  • Sengoku 2. Sword is the default weapon with high/low attacks and a parry; bosses are larger and mark story points. Stage-by-stage boss lists were not found.

Not verified: the exact enemy roster of each Final Fight stage beyond the first three, Sengoku mid-bosses, and Arcade Stadium specifics beyond the shared features above.

Depth (beat 'em up convention, from community dev guides, not Final Fight's own code): characters walk a floor band, attacks test a depth tolerance first and then the usual box overlap, and a thin tolerance makes hits miss unless fighters are nearly aligned, so the tolerance is kept generous (14 units) and the CPU aligns itself to the target.

Mapping: five stages (not six) of three thug waves plus a boss, carried life with recovery between waves and stages (food), three credits (continues). Breakable objects, food pickups and two bonus rounds are implemented with original content (see Stage objects); weapons and rewind are not.

Rust engine UI references

Study of the eleven Rust engines listed in "Best Rust Game Engine for Game Development" (WeeTech Solution, 2026) and what is worth borrowing for menus, loading screens, HUD, settings and buttons. Nothing is copied into this repository. Only ideas and layout patterns are recorded here.

Stack constraints that bind every recommendation: wgpu + winit renderer, tiny-skia, custom immediate-mode UI in src/ui.rs and src/app/menu_view.rs, layout tokens in src/ui_tokens.rs. No macroquad, no egui, no Lua.

Method and limits

  • Source was read only for five repositories, shallow-cloned at the session's read access: not-fl3/macroquad (MIT OR Apache-2.0), ggez/ggez (MIT), FyroxEngine/Fyrox (MIT), bevyengine/bevy (MIT OR Apache-2.0), AmbientRun/ambient (MIT OR Apache-2.0). Licence text was confirmed from the repository files.
  • The other six (Amethyst, Piston, Nannou, Blue Engine, Tetra, rend3) were not opened. Their notes below come from the article only and are marked as unverified.
  • The article itself is marketing text. Its descriptions are generic and some claims (for example, which engines are actively maintained) were not checked.

Engine by engine

EngineLicenceUI relevanceWhat we can use
MacroquadMIT OR Apache-2.0High. Immediate-mode UI in src/ui/ (widgets, style.rs, key_repeat.rs, combobox, clipboard.rs, input_handler.rs)Closest model to our UI. Key-repeat for held arrows in menus, a style/skin struct for button and panel colours, combobox behaviour for settings. Stack rule: we do not adopt the crate.
FyroxMITHigh. fyrox-ui is a full retained-mode widget set: buttons, dropdown list, dropdown menu, tab control, scroll viewer, progress bar, message box, popup, file browser, navigation, styleReference for the set of widgets a settings screen needs, focus navigation.rs for keyboard and gamepad, progress_bar for loading, messagebox for confirm dialogs, and a style module for themes. Retained-mode message passing does not fit our immediate-mode code, so ideas only.
BevyMIT OR Apache-2.0Medium. bevy_ui (flexbox), bevy_ui_render, bevy_ui_widgets (headless widgets, behaviour separated from styling)The split between widget behaviour and visual style is worth copying conceptually. Flexbox is not needed; our 1280x720 virtual layout with tokens is enough. Bevy's state-based screen flow suggests how to structure loading and transitions.
AmbientMIT OR Apache-2.0Low to medium. A UI element tree (element, element_component) built on its own runtimeOnly the idea of composing small reusable elements (button, panel, label) with props. Its runtime is too large to borrow from.
GGEZMITLow. No UI layer; has a graphics text/glyph path and timersReference for a minimal loop and text rendering with glyph caching. Nothing to copy for UI chrome.
Tetranot checkedLow (article only)Nothing needed beyond what we have.
Amethystnot checkedLow (article only). Project status should be checked before any referenceSkip.
Pistonnot checkedLow (article only)Skip.
Nannounot checkedLow (article only; creative coding, not a game UI)Skip.
Blue Enginenot checkedLow (article only)Skip.
rend3not checkedLow (renderer only, no UI)Skip. Its post-processing ideas are covered by our own postfx.

Prioritised recommendations

Ordered by player-visible impact and by how little they cost to build on the current UI code.

  1. Loading screen with a progress bar and tips. Fyrox's progress_bar and Macroquad's simple panel style show the pattern. We already have src/loading_tips.rs; add a determinate bar driven by the real load stages (parallel load already exists, see Performance). Expected result: loading no longer looks frozen.
  2. Keyboard and gamepad focus navigation with key-repeat. Macroquad's key_repeat.rs and Fyrox's navigation.rs. Holding up/down in menus should step smoothly, and focus should be visible on every screen.
  3. Settings widgets: dropdown, tabs, scroll viewer. Fyrox's dropdown_list, tab_control, scroll_viewer and Macroquad's combobox define the expected behaviour (open, close on outside click, keyboard selection). Put them in new files under src/ui/ or src/app/, using ui_tokens.
  4. Confirm dialogs and tooltips. Fyrox's messagebox and popup for "quit match?", "delete replay?" and similar prompts. Keeps destructive actions explicit.
  5. Theme struct for colours and sizes. Macroquad's style.rs and Fyrox's style module. We already have 11 themes in menu_art.rs; moving their values into one Theme struct with tokens makes adding a theme a data change.
  6. Screen transitions as a small state machine. Bevy's state pattern. Fade or slide between title, select, fight and results, with easing matching the existing menu entry animation (ease-out cubic, 0.28 s).
  7. Headless widget behaviour. Bevy's bevy_ui_widgets idea: separate hit-testing and focus logic from drawing so the same button logic serves the menu, pause and settings screens.

Status against the current code

The recommendations above were checked against the code on 2026-11-10. Most of the list already exists, so the work is to keep it and fill the real gaps.

ItemStatus
Loading screen with progress bar and tipsAlready there: Ui::loading_screen, progress_bar, src/loading_tips.rs, real step labels in src/app/loading.rs. Keep.
Smooth menu focusAlready there: src/app/menu_focus.rs (frame-rate independent easing). Keep.
Confirm dialogsPresent for replay deletion in replay_browser.rs; pause has its own skin. Other destructive actions could reuse the pattern.
Screen transitionsAlready there: diagonal wipe in src/app.rs. Keep.
Key repeat when a direction is heldWas missing: the shell drops OS key repeats on purpose, so menus and sliders moved one step per tap. Added in src/controls/nav_repeat.rs (0.38 s delay, then every 75 ms, directions only).
Dropdown, tabs, tooltips, theme structNot implemented. Candidates for later small PRs.

What we will not do

  • Adopt macroquad, egui or any engine's runtime. That breaks the stack decision in Engine.
  • Copy code from MIT or Apache-2.0 sources into the repo. Use them as design references only, so no licence notice is needed.
  • Touch character sprites or stages. Those are handled elsewhere.

Authoring tool survey: Fighter Factory Studio

Static study of a public Windows build of Fighter Factory Studio (FFS 3, portable Qt4/Qt5 package, about 2000 files, 57 MB). It is the reference editor of the MUGEN community, so it shows what authors expect when they create characters. Nothing from the package is copied into this repository; only formats, checks and workflow conclusions are recorded here.

Method and limits

  • The archive was extracted into an empty folder and only inspected: file listing, XML/HTML/Lua data files and strings on the engine-module DLL. No binary was executed.
  • REA (rea-agents 6.8.0) installs and runs, but native decompilation needs Hopper, Ghidra, IDA or Rizin, none of which exist in this environment. Native analysis was therefore limited to string tables. A later pass with a provider could decompile ff.mugen.dll to confirm the exact rule behind each message.

Disassembly pass (radare2)

Hopper and IDA are commercial and Ghidra's host is blocked by the network policy; Rizin is not in the package repositories. radare2 5.5 (Ubuntu) was used instead, read-only on the 32-bit ff.mugen.dll, nothing executed. Confirmed so far: the guard handler branches on the defender state type, value 1 enters state 150, 2 enters 152, 3 enters 154 (the reaction to a guarded hit; state names should be checked against the target engine's common1), anything else prints "Guard state error: wrong move type". So the warning is about the defender's statetype, not the attacker's movetype. The remaining messages are still unconfirmed against code.

What the package contains

AreaFinding
Editor modulesSprites (SFF 1/2, onion skin, layers), Animations (visual and code), Palettes, Sounds, Commands, States, Definitions, Emulator and Debug workspaces
ScriptingLua 5.3 scripts for editor automation (scripts/tool, scripts/project)
Engine moduleOne module per engine (engines/mugen): schema, completion list, one template file per state controller (89), snippets, project templates, per-version docs (1.0, 1.1, common, DOS, Win)
EmulatorAn in-editor MUGEN-compatible runtime (MUGENext) with training mode, breakpoints by file and line, variable inspection

Declarative schema (syntax.xml)

The whole .def/.cns/.cmd/.air grammar is data, not code. It covers nine file kinds (char, state, command, stage, fight, select, motif, font, storyboard) and almost 3000 parameters. Each parameter has a name and a type (int, float, int2, int4, intvec, expi, expf, expb, keyword, ustring, file, hitattr, hitflags, guardflags, keyseq), plus optional attributes: required, optional, minver, deprecated, list, max. Examples of required fields: StateDef needs type, movetype, physics, anim; [Data] needs life, attack, defence, fall.defence_up, liedown.time, airjuggle.

Lint messages driven by that schema: duplicate parameter in a group, invalid block for the project type, parameter invalid for the project version, parameter deprecated since version X, wrong argument count, duplicate or invalid hit attribute and hit flag, invalid keyword, trigger redirection invalid in this context, syntax error with line.

Asset checks

  • Required sprite missing (group, index) when loading a character.
  • Palette or sprite entry without id, file, axis or palette; invalid NPOT mode.
  • Duplicate palettes (noDuplicatePal, "remove all duplicates") and unused palettes ("clear unused").
  • 32-colour palettes stored as 5-bit data; palette remap table.

Runtime warnings of the emulator

Each warning carries tick, player, state and file: line: change to an invalid state, action or anim element; guard state with the wrong move type; invalid RemapPal in Helper or Explod; Explod bind id not found; invalid PalFX time, colour or multiplier; trigger redirection problems; invalid AI file ignored.

Workflow features worth matching

  1. Sprite import by file name with group and index (group_index, group-index, group,index), axis presets, three palette modes (own palette, force palette, exchange palette), crop before or after the axis.
  2. Aligned export with one common axis ("perfect axis") plus onion skin while aligning.
  3. Sprite explorer: create an animation straight from selected thumbnails.
  4. Per-frame loop point, scale, angle and interpolation flags.
  5. Variable usage list and log per state file (var, fvar, sysvar collisions between states and helpers).
  6. Snippets and state controller templates for common moves.

Gap against our skills and tools

The mugen-character-creator skill had no pre-flight checklist for required or version-gated parameters, palette hygiene, variable collisions, or import naming, and no mapping of runtime warnings to causes. The new reference references/checklist_lint_editor.md adds it, and the skill now points to it.

Follow-ups (code, not done here)

  • Drive mugen_check from a schema of required, version-gated and deprecated parameters written from the public MUGEN documentation.
  • Add a variable usage report (var, fvar, sysvar) across states and helpers.
  • Add palette duplicate and unused reports next to sprite_audit.
  • Accept group_index style names in import_sprite_atlas.
  • Print the runtime warnings above, with state and line, in the debug overlay.

Reverse engineering a browser M.U.G.E.N port

English · Português (BR)

What https://w8.snokido.com/games/html5/dbz-vs-marvel-vs-capcom/ does with a 78-fighter M.U.G.E.N roster, how its animation system works, why it holds 60 fps, and what of all that we should copy — or not — in Ultimate MUGEN.

Everything below was measured or read from the shipped artifacts. The scripts that produced it live in docs/research/ikemen-web/, so every number can be re-run.

1. What the page is

The public page is a 11 KB shell: menus, character select, versus splash and the options screens are plain DOM (that part is the snokido/runtime-ui.js UI layer). The fight itself is a separate document, frame.html, inside an iframe, and the engine there is not JavaScript: it is a Go program compiled to WebAssembly.

ArtifactSizeRole
index.html11 KBshell: boot, menu, select, options
local-runtime.js342 KBobfuscated bootstrap: holds the Go wasm_exec glue and the frame module as strings, plus the content catalog
runtime-ui.js420 KBthe DOM UI (obfuscated, digest-gated)
frame.html2.2 KBengine host: one <canvas id="ikemen-canvas">
runtime-engine.bin5,887,387 Bgzip of a 25,343,508 B WebAssembly module
content/catalog.shvd.json265 KB78 characters, 74 stages, pack URLs, sha256, sizes
content/packs/*.zip1–24 MB eachunmodified M.U.G.E.N files, one zip per character/stage

The bootstrap posts {frameJs, wasmExec, descriptor, gzipBytes} to frame.html, which installs wasm_exec.js from a string, imports the engine module from a Blob URL and gates it on a SHA-256 of the values it was handed. That is copy protection, not engine design.

$ node docs/research/ikemen-web/wasm-artifacts.js runtime-engine.bin
module bytes: 25343508
[imports "gojs"] 25
  runtime.scheduleTimeoutEvent:function
  runtime.wasmExit:function
  syscall/js.valueGet:function
  syscall/js.copyBytesToJS:function
  mem:memory
[exports] run:function resume:function getsp:function mem:memory
[build info] ikemen-GO v0.0.0-20260927200105-cae6cd63ba4a+dirty
[go source files named by the symbol table] ... render_webgl.go render_webgl_cmdbuf.go system_js.go audio_js.go input_js.go loadyield_js.go ...

gojs imports plus run/resume/getsp exports are the Go runtime's WebAssembly ABI, and the Go symbol table keeps every source path. The engine is Ikemen-GO (the open Go reimplementation of M.U.G.E.N) with a WebGL2 backend added for the browser: render_webgl.go, render_webgl_cmdbuf.go, system_js.go, audio_js.go, input_js.go, pause_js.go, platform_js.go, loadyield_js.go, font_webgl.go, netplay_js.go.

The catalog names its own provenance, which is how the backend source was located and cross-checked against the binary:

"source": { "components": [
  { "name": "ikemen-go-web",      "url": "https://github.com/energyjp/ikemen-go-web",             "revision": "54305ec917c3e995f433004e2e8f7c8902bff96a" },
  { "name": "Ikemen-GO-Screenpack","url": "https://github.com/ikemen-engine/Ikemen-GO-Screenpack", "revision": "87f348a5f6e01e878a62ae865c6ee7d3281f8c98" } ] }

Upstream ikemen-engine/Ikemen-GO has no WebGL backend; energyjp/ikemen-go-web does. The checked-out source matches the binary exactly (opcode table, GLSL, symbol names, canvas id), so the "how" below is verified against both.

2. Content: no re-encoding, just zips

The packs contain the original M.U.G.E.N files — .def, .sff, .snd, .air, .cns, .zss, .act — untouched. Verified on the Goku pack (24,319,368 B, sha256 matches the catalog): files/goku.sff 9.6 MB, files/goku-jap-en-bl.snd 20.7 MB, files/goku.air 287 KB, 21 palette .png/.act files, plus the character's own movelist HTML.

So the browser downloads raw M.U.G.E.N content and the WASM engine parses SFF/SND by itself. Nothing is pre-baked into spritesheets, and only the front-end media (portraits, icons, stage thumbnails) is pre-encoded to WebP with content-addressed names (collections/shvd/media/<sha256>.webp).

core (7.0 MB zip → 9.7 MB) is the screenpack and system data, and every other pack declares "dependencies": ["core"]. A match loads: core + one pack per fighter + one pack per stage.

3. Animation: M.U.G.E.N semantics, unchanged

Animations are .air files parsed into the same structures M.U.G.E.N uses (src/anim.go):

StructureFields that matter
Animationframes, loopstart, curtime, curelem, totaltime, looptime, interpolate_offset/scale/angle/blend, mask, transType, srcAlpha/dstAlpha
AnimFrameGroup, Number, Xoffset, Yoffset, Time (ticks), Xscale/Yscale, Angle, TransType, Clsn1/Clsn2
Anim (instance)anim, x/y, xscl/yscl, window, xshear, rot, palfx, layerno, localcoord

The per-tick path is deliberately cheap:

  1. Animation.Action() advances curtime; at totaltime it jumps to loopstart and sets newframe.
  2. Animation.UpdateSprite() runs every tick but only does work when newframe is set — that is where the sprite is resolved, with one map lookup: a.spr = a.sff.GetSprite(uint16(group), uint16(number)) (anim.go:702), after applying the character's Remap presets.
  3. Rendering reads frames[drawidx] for the transform and the cached spr for the texture. Nothing is re-looked-up per tick, and nothing is interpolated.

So there is no tweening and no sub-tick interpolation: frames change on the 60 Hz tick, exactly like M.U.G.E.N. The perceived smoothness comes from the tick rate, from interpolate offset/scale/angle/blend (which animate transforms between AIR frames), and from the shader doing all colour work in one pass.

Colour is a shader feature, not a bake

Two things that would normally cost uploads are pushed into the fragment shader (src/shaders/sprite.frag.glsl, which is also embedded in the WASM as a string):

c = COMPAT_TEXTURE(tex, uv);
if (isRgba) { ... } else {
    c = COMPAT_TEXTURE(pal, vec2(c.r*0.9966, 0.5));   // palette lookup from the red channel
}
if (hue  != 0.0) c.rgb = hue_shift(c.rgb, hue);
if (neg)         c.rgb = neg_base - c.rgb;
c.rgb = mix(vec3((c.r+g.c+b)/3.0), c.rgb, 1.0 - gray);
c.rgb += final_add;
c *= final_mul;
if (!isFlat) c.rgb = mix(c.rgb, tint.rgb * c.a, tint.a);
  • Palettes: an indexed sprite keeps its 8-bit pixels as the texture and is coloured through a 256×1 palette texture (newPaletteTexture() → newTexture(256, 1, 32, false)). Changing pal1…pal12 or RemapPal re-uploads 1 KB, not the sprite. Sprite::CachePalTex (image.go:1336) compares the 256 colour words and only re-uploads on change, so a palette swap costs one texSubImage2D per sprite that actually changes.
  • palFX (add, mul, color, hue, invertall) is per-sprite uniforms on the same draw — no second pass, no RenderMode shader switching.
  • Trapezoid distortion (floor shadows / xscale skew) is computed in the same shader from gl_FragCoord, not by re-projecting vertices.

One shader covers flat quads, RGBA sprites, indexed sprites, trapezoids and the whole palFX chain. M.U.G.E.N's "one more shader per effect" problem simply does not exist there.

4. How it stays fast

The interesting part. Measured on the shipped build (headless Chromium, ANGLE/SwiftShader so the GPU numbers are software-rendered, 1280×720 CSS, two runs on a loaded machine):

MetricValue
Canvas backing store640×480 (CSS 1280×720, object-fit: contain)
drawArrays per rAFp50 82–105, p95 113–163, max 172–224
bufferData per rAF82–125 (one small upload per sprite; runs of text share one)
Uniform calls per rAF322–397
useProgram per second30–76 (a handful per frame)
bindTexture per second1.4k–6.2k
Engine frames per rAF0.78–0.89 (fixed 60 Hz, gated)
JS heap in a match9–74 MB
Boot → menu1.9 s
Menu → select4.0 s
Select → first fight37 s (core + 2 fighter packs + stage over the network, then SFF decode)
Long tasks during a match50–90 ms, recurring (asset decode / GC on the main thread)

4.1 The scene renders at 640×480 into an FBO, then gets blitted

Init() creates an RGBA texture + a DEPTH_COMPONENT24 renderbuffer at sys.scrrect (640×480) and draws the whole scene there; EndFrame() runs the external post shaders through two ping-pong FBOs and only then does one drawArrays(TRIANGLE_STRIP, 0, 4) to the default framebuffer with a letterboxed viewport and NEAREST (or LINEAR if the user picked smoothed scaling). Every sprite is rasterized at 640×480 regardless of window size.

4.2 One JS crossing per frame instead of one per GL call

This is the headline trick (render_webgl_cmdbuf.go). GL calls are not issued from Go; they are encoded into a byte stream:

// GL command buffer: batches the browser build's per-frame WebGL commands into a shared ArrayBuffer
// that a JS-side interpreter drains in ONE syscall/js crossing per flush, instead of one crossing
// per GL command.
//
// Why: profiling the shipped (v0.9) build showed hundreds of `gl.Call` crossings per frame; each
// crossing boxes its arguments through syscall/js.makeValue (~450MB/30s of JS garbage) and pays the
// wasm->JS context switch.
  • 256 KB staging buffer (wglCmdBufBytes = 1 << 18), 23 opcodes (useProgram, uniform*, activeTexture+bindTexture, bufferData, drawArrays, enable/disable, blendFunc, scissor, depthMask, bindVertexArray, texParameteri, …).
  • GL objects (textures, programs, uniform locations, VAOs, buffers) are registered once into a JS array and referenced by integer handle.
  • flushCmds() does one js.CopyBytesToJS + one Invoke of a JS interpreter built with the Function constructor.
  • Every direct GL call goes through glc(), which flushes first, so command order is preserved by construction.

4.3 Uniform and state deduplication on the Go side

SetUniformISub/SetUniformFSub keep per-program caches keyed by (programID << 16) | uniformIndex and emit nothing when the value is unchanged. EnableBlending, SetDepthTest, SetDepthMask, EnableScissor and ChangeProgram do the same for GL state. That is why ~14 uniforms per sprite collapse to ~4 on average, and why useProgram is only 30–50 calls per second.

4.4 Zero allocation in the draw path

The same file documents the measured cost of the naive version: passing a local [16]float32 to an interface method made it escape, allocating vertices + uniform + modelview per quad, and drawQuads alone allocated >1 GB per 30 s of heap. The fix is package-level scratch arrays reused per call (the render path is single-threaded and each buffer is consumed synchronously).

4.5 rAF gating to the game's framerate

system_js.go does not run a frame per requestAnimationFrame; it runs at most one per 1000/Video.Framerate:

// Browsers fire rAF at the DISPLAY's refresh rate - 120/144/240Hz on high-refresh screens. ...
// Releasing a frame on every rAF therefore runs the whole loop 2-4x more often than the game is
// authored for, multiplying allocation and forcing far more frequent GC pauses (the 200-500ms
// mark stalls high-refresh users saw) for zero visual benefit.

SwapBuffers() then parks the main goroutine on a channel until the next released frame — which also yields the JS event loop so input, network and audio callbacks run.

4.6 Sprites are not atlased; fonts are

Every sprite keeps its own texture. There is no sprite atlas and no eviction policy, so a match can never hit an atlas-full cliff. The 16 texture units are used as an LRU cache (texCacheTexSerial/texCacheLastUsed) so consecutive sprites from the same sheet do not re-bind.

Only text uses a TextureAtlas: 256×256, skyline packing with edge extrusion, and glyph quads batched per atlas so a run of text is one draw.

4.7 One draw call per sprite, by design

SetVertexData(...16 floats...) + RenderQuad() → bufferData(STATIC_DRAW) followed by drawArrays(TRIANGLE_STRIP, 0, 4). Per sprite: 1 bufferData, 1 drawArrays, ~4 uniforms, ≤1 texture bind — all inside the command buffer, so the Go side pays only a few emitI/emitF per sprite. At 82–172 sprites per frame that is 5–10 k GL calls/s, which is exactly what a software rasterizer in headless Chromium can absorb.

5. What we already do better

Ultimate MUGEN does not need the command buffer: our shell talks to wgpu, which already packs a frame into a few submissions. And our sprite path is architecturally ahead of theirs:

ConcernIkemen web buildUltimate MUGEN
Draw calls1 per sprite (82–172/frame)batched: quads merged per blend state + scissor into one vertex/index buffer
Bind stateper-sprite texture binds, 16-unit LRUone bind group; atlases + palette texture bound once
Palette256×1 texture per sprite, per-sprite upload on change1024 palette rows in one texture, row index per vertex, RemapPal swaps the row
Atlasnone for sprites (per-sprite textures)RGBA atlas + 8-bit index atlas, reset independently
Simulationwhole fighter state machine in WASMhotpath_bench (below)
Frame pacingrAF gate at Video.Framerateume_shell::Pacer + fixed 60 Hz step (≤5 ticks/frame)

Our simulation cost, so the frame budget is not the issue:

$ cargo run --release -p ume-engine --example hotpath_bench
sff decode                   mean      829.6 us
air parse                    mean      493.5 us
cns parse+compile            mean     3680.8 us
char load (no images)        mean     7388.2 us
match tick (2 fighters)      mean        4.2 us   p99  9.0
match tick (6 fighters)      mean       11.3 us   p99 17.6
match tick (10 fighters)     mean       20.1 us   p99 33.5

4–20 µs per tick against a 16.7 ms frame: 0.03–0.12 %. The fight is spent in the renderer and the loader, which is exactly where the browser port spent its effort too.

6. What we changed

The port's own bug reports (>1 GB/30 s of GC from per-quad allocations, 450 MB/30 s from per-call boxing, 200–500 ms stalls from oversimulating at 144 Hz) all have the same shape: a whole match's work paid inside one frame. We had the same shape in one place: the sprite warm-up.

App::finish_fight uploaded fighter sprites in the single frame that switched to the fight:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
self.g.trim(4000);
for f in &sess.m.fighters { if !self.g.prefetch(&f.def, 0.5) { break; } }
}

How much art a fighter carries (new sprite_mem example):

$ cargo run --release -p ume-engine --example sprite_mem -- mugen/chars/BuuZ2 mugen/chars/cell mugen/chars/frieza
mugen:c/buuz2.def   sprites=2510  indexed=2510 | index atlas  33.71 MB | total  33.86 MB | largest spr 5202 KB
mugen:c/cell.def    sprites=631   indexed=631  | index atlas   9.91 MB | total   9.99 MB | largest spr  818 KB
mugen:c/frieza.def  sprites=673   indexed=673  | index atlas   8.67 MB | total   8.74 MB | largest spr  682 KB

A DBZ pair is 43.6 MB of index sheets across 3,141 sprites, and the largest single sprite is 1.3 MB.

6.1 Pay the warm-up per frame, not per match

App::warm_step + Gfx::prefetch_step: a load step of its own that copies at most WARM_BUDGET = 512 KiB per call. Behind the VS screen it is one chunk per frame (the splash lasts at least 1.8 s), and the blocking start_fight path (rematch from the pause menu or the results screen, netplay start, the scripted tours) now yields a frame between chunks instead of freezing.

Measured on the same machine, same tour, same fighters, with UME_WATCHDOG=1:

Damaging frame
before212.8 ms in 'fight:prefetch' (one frame)
after2.3 / 2.4 / 2.5 / 2.1 / 8.8 ms in 'load:sprites' (one chunk per frame)

A rematch with the same roster no longer flushes the texture cache at all (see 6.3), so its warm-up copies nothing.

6.2 Palette rows are shared by content

ume_render::PaletteRows keeps one row per distinct 256-colour palette instead of one row per palette object: a mirror match, a RemapPal that lands on an existing palette, and a re-warm after an atlas reset all reuse the row and skip the upload. Unit-tested in crates/render/src/palette.rs (50 lookups of the same colours → one row; a full atlas reports failure instead of overwriting a row in use).

6.3 A rematch keeps the atlases it already filled

The warm-up keys on the roster (def.id of both fighters). If the key matches the last warm-up, Gfx::trim is skipped, so the atlas generation does not change and prefetch_step finds every sprite already resident: the second fight of a marathon starts with zero uploads.

6.4 A draw-call budget that fails the build

ume_render::DRAW_CALL_BUDGET = 24 with batch::tests::a_fight_screen_stays_within_the_draw_call_budget: a synthetic fight frame (stage layers, a subtractive reflection pass, two fighters, additive hit sparks, a two-region HUD overlay) must stay under the ceiling, and a_flat_run_of_quads_is_one_call pins the 300-quads-one-call property. Break the batching and CI says so.

6.5 Hitch labels that point at the right phase

ume_shell::watchdog::label now sticks to the first phase named in a frame. Before, the trailing label("import") at the end of App::frame overwrote everything, so a slow loading step was reported as an import; that is why the load:sprites numbers above are visible at all. Unit-tested.

6.6 What the numbers also told us

prefetch_step logs where it stops: for a native (RGBA, high-resolution) fighter the 50 % atlas cap fits 8 of 116 sprites, after which the warm-up gives up and the rest stream lazily during the fight — one upload at draw time, which is what the browser port does for every sprite. For indexed DBZ art the same cap fits a few hundred. So the bulk warm-up is bounded by the atlas, not by the roster, and the next step (backlog 5) is to give the lazy path a per-frame upload budget instead of trying to pre-load more.

7. Backlog, in priority order

#Idea from the portState hereHow to verify
1Never pay a whole match inside one framedone: App::warm_step + Gfx::prefetch_step, 512 KiB per frame, VS step and start_fight both spreadUME_WATCHDOG=1 label load:sprites; F3 up/KB
2Keep the transition frame free in the paths with no VS screendone: start_fight yields a frame per chunkUME_WATCHDOG=1 worst frame at the transition

7b. Are we better than them?

On the things this investigation measured, yes — and on the things it did not measure, no. Being precise matters more than the headline.

Better:

So: a better engine on the measured axes, and a smaller product than theirs. The PR that follows implements every item of section 7 that was still open.

8. Reproducing

# artifacts, request order, sizes, frame list
NODE_PATH="$(npm root -g)" node docs/research/ikemen-web/capture.js capture

# what the engine module needs, exports, and which Go files it was built from
NODE_PATH="$(npm root -g)" node docs/research/ikemen-web/wasm-artifacts.js capture/runtime-engine.bin

# per-frame WebGL counters from inside frame.html
NODE_PATH="$(npm root -g)" node docs/research/ikemen-web/frame-stats.js

capture/ then holds the gzipped engine, the UI bundles, the catalog and the content packs used above. Playwright and Chromium are required; nothing is pulled from a third-party package registry beyond them.

Two measurement caveats: the numbers come from headless Chromium with SwiftShader (a software rasterizer), so treat the frame times as a floor, not a GPU result; and the 37 s select→fight time is dominated by the download of ~50 MB of content in that sandbox, not by the engine's own parsing.

Character tuning

Settings → Gameplay → Character tuning changes per-character parameters without touching the original files. Values are percentages (100% = unchanged), kept in char_tuning.toml next to the executable (web: browser storage).

ParameterApplies toMechanism
LifeMUGEN and UMEdata.life
Damage dealtMUGEN and UMEdata.attack (fighter attack multiplier)
Damage takenMUGEN and UMEtuning.defence read by the fighter defence multiplier
Walk, run, jumpMUGEN and UMEvelocity.* constants
GravityMUGEN and UMEmovement.yaccel
Power barMUGEN and UMEdata.power
Energy costMUGEN and UMEnegative PowerAdd values scaled by tuning.power_cost

Ranges are 25–300% (power bar and energy cost 0–300%). A character with all values at 100% is not written to the file. Reset a character with "Reset to default".

File format:

["native:kaito"]
life = 150
defence = 75

Code: src/char_tuning/ (model, store, tests), src/registry/tuning.rs (applied when a character is stored), src/app/char_tuning_screen.rs (screen).

Cinematic cameras

The first-round intro and every round-win pose run a short camera shot made of beats. The shot is a pure function of the match clock, so replays and rollback stay deterministic.

  • Beats live in assets/cinematic.toml. A copy named cinematic.toml next to the settings file replaces the [[intro]] and [[victory]] sections it defines; an invalid file is ignored.
  • Each beat: subject (p1, p2, both, winner), duration seconds, ease (linear, in, out, in_out, back), and [from, to] pairs for zoom (added to the stage zoom), focus (0 wide to 1 on the subject), shake (trauma), sweep (world px camera truck, gives background parallax) and, for 3D fighters only, yaw (orbit, radians), pitch (negative = low angle, positive = crane from above, radians), lens (0 to 0.6 perspective emphasis, nearer parts grow) and detail + aim (extra model zoom, 0 to 2 = up to 3x, rendered 1:1 in a sharper 640px window centred on a body height: 0 feet, 0.85 face, 0.6 sword arm).
  • Values are clamped, so a bad file cannot break the view. enabled = false turns every shot off.
  • Fighters without a 3D model get the same zoom and pan on their sprites; 3D fighters also orbit.
  • The intro shot ends when the existing intro skip fires; Reduce motion disables zoom, pan, shake and orbit.
  • Smoke: node scripts/web-cinematic-smoke.js web/dist (needs bash scripts/build-web.sh).

Combo Trials

Training mode shows a ladder of seven combo goals above the arena. They work for every fighter, native or M.U.G.E.N, because they only read the combo counters the engine already keeps.

#Goal
13 hits
25 hits
38 hits
425% of the rival's life in one combo
56 or more hits finishing with a super (at least 1000 power spent)
610 or more hits without spending any meter
745% of the rival's life in one combo

A combo is judged when it ends. Goals are cleared in order, a flash says TRIAL CLEAR and progress is saved per fighter in trials.json (next to the config, or in browser storage on the web build). Finishing the ladder shows ALL TRIALS CLEARED.

How it works

  • src/trials.rs: pure Tracker, fed once per frame with the player's combo_count, combo_damage, power and the rival's life_max. It tracks power at the start and the lowest power during the combo to know whether meter was spent.
  • src/app/trials_hud.rs: reads the match after each tick (never changes it) and draws the panel; hidden while paused, in replays and outside training.
  • Tracker::demo replaces the live sample and exists only for the screenshot tour: UME_SHOTS_ONLY=trials.
  • Cost: one struct update per frame in training only; no allocation.

Kit Inputs

Português (BR)

Native fighters no longer share one input set. Each archetype swaps some quarter-circle motions for inputs that fit its style. The move list in the pause menu shows the real input of every move.

FighterMoveInputStyle
ValdricSovereignhold back 40 ticks, forward + yCharge (zone control)
VoltaTeslahold back 40 ticks, forward + yCharge (zoner)
BrunoLariat360° motion + yGrappler, command throw
DaichiAura Rush360° motion + xGrappler rush

Charge motions use the ~40$B, F, x syntax and work in the training mode, versus and online. Air variants of a move need a motion that can be done in the air, so charge inputs are kept for ground-only moves.

Air mobility

stats.airDashes sets how many air dashes a fighter has before landing (default 1). Rushdown and aerial fighters get more, grapplers fewer.

FighterAir dashes
Suzume, Jin, Akio, Lian, Kaito2
Bruno0
Everyone else1

Rekka follow-ups

A move can only start from another move by declaring rekka in the character JSON:

{"id":"gust_cross","name":"Gust Crossup","input":"b","kind":"special","anim":"mirage","rekka":{"after":["gustdash"],"window":[6,20]}}

after lists the source move ids, window is the range of state time (ticks inside the source move, hit pause does not count) where the follow-up input is accepted, and contact: true also requires the source to hit or be guarded. Without it the follow-up works on whiff too. The follow-up never starts from neutral, so it may reuse a plain button already used by a normal. Code: crates/native/src/rekka.rs.

In use: Lian (Flowing Silk Kicks, then y), Kaito (Storm Rush, then x) and Jin (Gust Dash, then b).

Distance and state requirements

requires also accepts distance (pixels between the bodies, min and/or max) and enemyState (air, ground, crouch, down, hit or attack). Two moves can share one input and the engine picks by situation, as long as the conditions do not overlap. A variant must come before the move it overrides in the moves list, because the first move that fits wins.

In use: Daichi (Landslide Point Blank within 55 pixels, otherwise Landslide Heel) and Bruno (Bull Catch against an airborne enemy, otherwise Bulldozer Rush).

Known partial items

  • DestroySelf: recursive also destroys the helpers it spawned, and removeexplods removes the explods it owns (semantics follow the Ikemen GO documentation).
  • Helper: inheritjuggle and size.xscale/sprpriority parameters are not read by the spawn path.
  • Explod: layerno = 1 behaves like ontop (per the Ikemen GO wiki). layerno = -1 and shadow are not read.
